32  Fourier Analysis as Change of Basis

(Poisson thread) On a periodic grid, Fourier modes exactly diagonalize the discrete Laplacian. With Dirichlet boundaries, the corresponding sine modes play the same role. This spectral viewpoint explains the conditioning and smoothing behavior observed in the Poisson chapters.

Fourier analysis provides the mathematical framework for decomposing functions, discrete signals, and linear operators into frequency components. In scientific computing, the Fourier transform diagonalizes shift-invariant operators, accelerates convolution from \(O(n^2)\) to \(O(n \log n)\) operations, and yields spectral differentiation methods with exponential convergence for smooth periodic solutions.

32.1 The Discrete Fourier Transform

We consider discrete signals defined on a uniform periodic grid of \(n\) points. The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) expands a vector in the orthonormal basis of discrete complex exponentials.

NoteDefinition: Periodic Grid Signal

A discrete signal \(\bx \in \fC^n\) represents samples of a periodic function on the uniform grid \(x_j = 2\pi j / n\) for \(j = 0, 1, ..., n-1\), with the periodic index convention \[ \begin{align} x_{j+n} = x_j \qquad \text{for all } j \in \fZ. \end{align} \]

NoteDefinition: DFT Matrix

Let \(\omega_n = e^{-2\pi i / n}\) denote the primitive \(n\)-th root of unity. The Discrete Fourier Transform matrix \(\bF \in \fC^{n \times n}\) has entries \[ \begin{align} F_{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} e^{-2\pi i j k / n}, \qquad 0 \leq j, k \leq n-1. \end{align} \] The forward transform maps a spatial signal \(\bx \in \fC^n\) to its frequency representation \(\hat{\bx} = \bF\bx\).

NoteLemma: Unitarity of the DFT Matrix

The normalized DFT matrix \(\bF\) is unitary: \[ \begin{align} \bF^* \bF = \bF \bF^* = \bI_n. \end{align} \] Consequently, the inverse transform is given by the conjugate transpose: \(\bF^{-1} = \bF^*\).

TipProof

We evaluate the \((j, \ell)\) entry of the Gram matrix product \(\bF^* \bF\). Because \((\bF^*)_{jk} = \overline{F_{kj}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-jk}\), we have \[ \begin{align} (\bF^* \bF)_{j\ell} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (\bF^*)_{jk} F_{k\ell} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega_n^{-jk} \omega_n^{k\ell} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \left( \omega_n^{\ell - j} \right)^k. \end{align} \] If \(j = \ell\), each term in the summation equals \(\omega_n^0 = 1\), yielding \(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 1 = 1\). If \(j \neq \ell\), let \(r = \omega_n^{\ell - j}\). Because \(-(n-1) \leq \ell - j \leq n-1\) and \(j \neq \ell\), the base \(r \neq 1\), while \(r^n = (\omega_n^n)^{\ell - j} = 1^{\ell - j} = 1\). The finite geometric series sums to \[ \begin{align} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} r^k = \frac{1 - r^n}{1 - r} = \frac{1 - 1}{1 - r} = 0. \end{align} \] Therefore, \((\bF^* \bF)_{j\ell} = \delta_{j\ell}\), which establishes \(\bF^* \bF = \bI_n\).

NoteTheorem: Parseval’s Identity and Isometry

The Discrete Fourier Transform is an isometry on \(\fC^n\) with respect to the Euclidean norm: \[ \begin{align} \|\bF\bx\|_2 = \|\bx\|_2 \qquad \text{for all } \bx \in \fC^n. \end{align} \] The inner product is likewise preserved: \(\langle \bF\bx, \bF\by \rangle = \langle \bx, \by \rangle\).

TipProof

Using the result above, the Euclidean norm of the transformed vector satisfies \[ \begin{align} \|\bF\bx\|_2^2 = (\bF\bx)^* (\bF\bx) = \bx^* \bF^* \bF \bx = \bx^* \bI \bx = \bx^* \bx = \|\bx\|_2^2. \end{align} \] Taking positive square roots proves the claim. For general vectors, \(\langle \bF\bx, \bF\by \rangle = (\bF\bx)^* (\bF\by) = \bx^* \bF^* \bF \by = \bx^* \by = \langle \bx, \by \rangle\).

NoteDefinition: Frequency Bins and Nyquist Limit

For a signal sampled on \(n\) points with uniform spacing \(h = 2\pi / n\), integer frequency index \(k\) corresponds to the continuous Fourier mode \(e^{ikx}\). The distinct resolvable frequencies are ordered as \[ \begin{align} 0, 1, 2, ..., \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, -\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor, ..., -1. \end{align} \] The maximum resolvable frequency is the Nyquist frequency \(k_{\text{Nyq}} = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\). Any continuous mode with frequency \(|k| > k_{\text{Nyq}}\) aliases to a lower grid frequency satisfying \(k' \equiv k \pmod n\).

TipRemark

(Normalization convention) Numerical libraries such as NumPy’s np.fft.fft define the forward transform without the factor \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so that \(\hat{\bx}_{\text{numpy}} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j \omega_n^{jk}\), and place the full factor \(1/n\) in the inverse transform np.fft.ifft. This choice scales the entries by \(\sqrt{n}\) relative to the unitary operator \(\bF\) defined here.

32.2 Circulant Matrices and the Convolution Theorem

A linear system or filtering operation that commutes with spatial translation is represented by a circulant matrix. The Discrete Fourier Transform diagonalizes every circulant matrix.

NoteDefinition: Circulant Matrix

Let \(\bc = (c_0, c_1, ..., c_{n-1})^T \in \fC^n\). The circulant matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc) \in \fC^{n \times n}\) has entries \(C_{jk} = c_{(j - k) \pmod n}\): \[ \begin{align} \mathbf{C} = \begin{pmatrix} c_0 & c_{n-1} & c_{n-2} & ... & c_1 \\ c_1 & c_0 & c_{n-1} & ... & c_2 \\ c_2 & c_1 & c_0 & ... & c_3 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ c_{n-1} & c_{n-2} & c_{n-3} & ... & c_0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \]

NoteTheorem: Spectral Diagonalization of Circulant Matrices

Every circulant matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc)\) is diagonalized by the unitary DFT matrix: \[ \begin{align} \mathbf{C} = \bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bF, \end{align} \] where the diagonal eigenvalue matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0, ..., \lambda_{n-1})\) has entries equal to the unnormalized DFT coefficients of the first column: \[ \begin{align} \lambda_k = \sqrt{n} (\bF\bc)_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \omega_n^{jk}. \end{align} \]

TipProof

Let \(\mathbf{S} = \operatorname{circ}(\be_2) \in \fR^{n \times n}\) be the cyclic permutation matrix that shifts coordinate indices forward by one: \(\mathbf{S}\bx = (x_{n-1}, x_0, x_1, ..., x_{n-2})^T\). Powers of \(\mathbf{S}\) shift indices by \(j\) positions, satisfying \(\mathbf{S}^n = \bI\). Every circulant matrix is a polynomial in \(\mathbf{S}\): \[ \begin{align} \mathbf{C} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \mathbf{S}^j. \end{align} \] Let \(\bv_k\) denote the \(k\)-th column of \(\bF^*\), with entries \((\bv_k)_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-jk}\). Multiplying by the shift matrix gives \[ \begin{align} (\mathbf{S}\bv_k)_j = (\bv_k)_{(j-1) \pmod n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-(j-1)k} = \omega_n^k \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-jk} \right) = \omega_n^k (\bv_k)_j. \end{align} \] Thus \(\bv_k\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with eigenvalue \(\omega_n^k\). Applying the polynomial representation of \(\mathbf{C}\) to \(\bv_k\) yields \[ \begin{align} \mathbf{C}\bv_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \mathbf{S}^j \bv_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j (\omega_n^k)^j \bv_k = \left( \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \omega_n^{jk} \right) \bv_k = \lambda_k \bv_k. \end{align} \] Collecting all \(n\) eigenvector equations in matrix form gives \(\mathbf{C}\bF^* = \bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\). Multiplying on the right by \(\bF\) yields \(\mathbf{C} = \bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bF\).

NoteTheorem: Discrete Convolution Theorem

Let \(\bc, \bx \in \fC^n\). The circular convolution \(\bz = \bc * \bx\) has components \[ \begin{align} z_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} c_k x_{(j - k) \pmod n} = (\mathbf{C}\bx)_j, \qquad \mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc). \end{align} \] Applying the Discrete Fourier Transform converts convolution to entrywise multiplication: \[ \begin{align} \bF(\bc * \bx) = \sqrt{n} (\bF\bc) \odot (\bF\bx), \end{align} \] where \(\odot\) denotes the Hadamard (entrywise) vector product.

TipProof

Because \(\bz = \mathbf{C}\bx\) and \(\mathbf{C} = \bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bF\) by the result above, we have \[ \begin{align} \bF\bz = \bF(\mathbf{C}\bx) = \bF(\bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bF \bx) = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\bF\bx). \end{align} \] Because \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is diagonal with entries \(\lambda_k = \sqrt{n}(\bF\bc)_k\), matrix-vector multiplication by \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) scales each component of \(\bF\bx\) by \(\sqrt{n}(\bF\bc)_k\): \[ \begin{align} (\bF\bz)_k = \lambda_k (\bF\bx)_k = \sqrt{n}(\bF\bc)_k (\bF\bx)_k. \end{align} \] Writing this component identity in vector form yields \(\bF(\bc * \bx) = \sqrt{n} (\bF\bc) \odot (\bF\bx)\).

32.3 The Fast Fourier Transform

Computing a matrix-vector product with a general dense \(n \times n\) matrix requires \(2n^2\) flops. The Cooley–Tukey Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) factors the DFT matrix into sparse structured factors, reducing the complexity to \(O(n \log n)\) operations.

NoteTheorem: Radix-2 Cooley–Tukey Decomposition

Let \(n\) be an even integer, and let \(\bx \in \fC^n\). Partition \(\bx\) into even-indexed and odd-indexed subvectors \(\bx_E, \bx_O \in \fC^{n/2}\) defined by \((\bx_E)_j = x_{2j}\) and \((\bx_O)_j = x_{2j+1}\) for \(j = 0, ..., n/2 - 1\). The \(n\)-point unnormalized DFT \(\hat{x}_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j \omega_n^{jk}\) satisfies the butterfly identity \[ \begin{align} \hat{x}_k &= (\hat{\bx}_E)_k + \omega_n^k (\hat{\bx}_O)_k, \\ \hat{x}_{k + n/2} &= (\hat{\bx}_E)_k - \omega_n^k (\hat{\bx}_O)_k, \end{align} \] for each \(k = 0, 1, ..., n/2 - 1\), where \(\hat{\bx}_E, \hat{\bx}_O\) are the \((n/2)\)-point DFTs of \(\bx_E\) and \(\bx_O\). When \(n = 2^p\), applying this reduction recursively requires \(O(n \log n)\) floating-point operations.

TipProof

Splitting the DFT sum into even and odd indices gives \[ \begin{align} \hat{x}_k = \sum_{m=0}^{n/2 - 1} x_{2m} \omega_n^{2mk} + \sum_{m=0}^{n/2 - 1} x_{2m+1} \omega_n^{(2m+1)k}. \end{align} \] Because \(\omega_n^2 = e^{-4\pi i / n} = e^{-2\pi i / (n/2)} = \omega_{n/2}\), the first sum is the \((n/2)\)-point transform of \(\bx_E\): \[ \begin{align} \sum_{m=0}^{n/2 - 1} x_{2m} \omega_{n/2}^{mk} = (\hat{\bx}_E)_k. \end{align} \] Factoring \(\omega_n^k\) out of the second sum gives \(\omega_n^k \sum_{m=0}^{n/2 - 1} x_{2m+1} \omega_{n/2}^{mk} = \omega_n^k (\hat{\bx}_O)_k\). This establishes the first identity: \[ \begin{align} \hat{x}_k = (\hat{\bx}_E)_k + \omega_n^k (\hat{\bx}_O)_k. \end{align} \] For the second half of the spectrum \(k + n/2\), the periodicity \(\omega_{n/2}^{m(k + n/2)} = \omega_{n/2}^{mk} (\omega_{n/2}^{n/2})^m = \omega_{n/2}^{mk}\) and the half-period phase shift \[ \begin{align} \omega_n^{k + n/2} = \omega_n^k \omega_n^{n/2} = \omega_n^k e^{-\pi i} = -\omega_n^k \end{align} \] give the complementary butterfly equation: \[ \begin{align} \hat{x}_{k + n/2} = (\hat{\bx}_E)_k - \omega_n^k (\hat{\bx}_O)_k. \end{align} \] In matrix form, introducing the diagonal twiddle matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n/2} = \operatorname{diag}(1, \omega_n, ..., \omega_n^{n/2-1})\) and the even–odd permutation matrix \(\bP_n\): \[ \begin{align} \hat{\bx} = \begin{pmatrix} \bI_{n/2} & \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n/2} \\ \bI_{n/2} & -\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n/2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \hat{\bx}_E \\ \hat{\bx}_O \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \bI_{n/2} & \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n/2} \\ \bI_{n/2} & -\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{n/2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{W}_{n/2} & \bzero \\ \bzero & \mathbf{W}_{n/2} \end{pmatrix} \bP_n \bx. \end{align} \] At each recursion stage, the butterfly recombination performs \(n/2\) complex multiplications and \(n\) additions. The arithmetic complexity satisfies the recurrence \[ \begin{align} T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + c n. \end{align} \] For \(n = 2^p\), the depth of the recursion tree is \(\log_2 n\), yielding total cost \(T(n) = c n \log_2 n = O(n \log n)\).

32.4 Spectral Differentiation

For smooth periodic functions, differentiation in the Fourier domain replaces finite-difference stencils with exact multiplication in frequency.

NoteTheorem: Spectral Differentiation of Periodic Functions

Let \(u: \fR \to \fC\) be a \(2\pi\)-periodic function with continuous derivatives through order \(m\). Representing \(u\) by its Fourier series \(u(x) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^\infty \hat{u}_k e^{ikx}\), the derivative has Fourier coefficients \[ \begin{align} \widehat{(u')}_k = ik \hat{u}_k. \end{align} \] If \(u\) is analytic in a strip \(\{z \in \fC : |\operatorname{Im}(z)| < d\}\), the truncation error of the discrete spectral derivative converges geometrically to zero: \[ \begin{align} \max_{x_j} |u'(x_j) - (D_n \bu)_j| = O(e^{-d n/2}). \end{align} \]

TipProof

Differentiating the series term by term gives \(\frac{d}{dx} \sum_{k} \hat{u}_k e^{ikx} = \sum_{k} (ik \hat{u}_k) e^{ikx}\), which proves the coefficient formula. If \(u\) is analytic in the strip of half-width \(d\), shifting the contour of integration in \(\hat{u}_k = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} u(x) e^{-ikx} dx\) to \(x - i \operatorname{sign}(k) d\) yields the bound \(|\hat{u}_k| \leq M e^{-d |k|}\). The aliased grid modes satisfy \(|k| \geq n/2\). Summing the tail of the neglected high-frequency modes gives \(\sum_{|k| \geq n/2} |k| |\hat{u}_k| \leq 2M \sum_{k=n/2}^\infty k e^{-d k} = O(e^{-d n/2})\).

32.5 Exercises

WarningExercise

  1. Check. Unitary coordinates and geometric sums. Let \(\bF \in \fC^{4 \times 4}\) be the 4-point DFT matrix. Write out its sixteen numerical entries explicitly using powers of \(\omega_4 = -i\). Verify directly that columns 0 and 2 are orthogonal, and confirm that \(\bF^* \bF = \bI_4\).

  2. Derive. Circulant spectral inversion for the periodic Poisson problem. Consider the discrete periodic Poisson equation \(-\frac{u_{j-1} - 2u_j + u_{j+1}}{h^2} = f_j\) on \(n\) points with periodic boundary conditions.

    1. Express the coefficient matrix as a circulant matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc)\) and identify the entries of \(\bc\).

    2. Compute the eigenvalues \(\lambda_k\) of \(\mathbf{C}\) using the result above. Show that \(\lambda_0 = 0\) and \(\lambda_k > 0\) for \(k = 1, ..., n-1\).

    3. Explain why the system is solvable if and only if \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j = 0\), and formulate an \(O(n \log n)\) solver using the FFT.

  3. Derive. Fast linear convolution via zero padding. Let \(\bx \in \fR^p\) and \(\by \in \fR^q\) be two discrete sequences. Their linear convolution has length \(m = p + q - 1\).

    1. Explain how zero-padding \(\bx\) and \(\by\) to length \(N \geq p + q - 1\) prevents periodic wraparound in circular convolution.

    2. Compare the arithmetic operation count of direct linear convolution (\(2pq\) flops) against FFT-based circular convolution (\(O(N \log N)\) flops).

    3. For \(p = q = 10^5\), estimate the speedup obtained by the FFT algorithm.

  4. Derive. Cooley–Tukey butterfly and bit-reversal permutation. Consider the radix-2 FFT algorithm with \(n = 8\).

    1. Write the indices \(0, 1, ..., 7\) in 3-bit binary notation (\(b_2 b_1 b_0\)).

    2. Reverse the bits (\(b_0 b_1 b_2\)) to construct the bit-reversal permutation vector \(\mathbf{p}\).

    3. Show that sorting the input by \(\mathbf{p}\) allows the recursive Cooley–Tukey butterflies to be evaluated in place without allocating auxiliary arrays.

  5. Compute. Spectral differentiation and the Runge phenomenon. Implement the Fourier spectral differentiation matrix for \(n = 16, 32, 64\) points on \([0, 2\pi)\).

    1. Apply the spectral derivative to \(u(x) = \sin(x)\) and measure the maximum pointwise error against \(\cos(x)\). Confirm that error reaches machine precision for small \(n\).

    2. Apply the spectral derivative to \(v(x) = \frac{1}{2 + \cos(x)}\). Estimate the decay constant \(d\) from the result above and confirm geometric convergence.

    3. Explain why applying Fourier differentiation to a non-periodic function such as \(w(x) = x\) causes Gibbs oscillations and algebraic error decay \(O(1/n)\).

NoteFurther reading

The Cooley–Tukey paper is short and still worth reading as an example of how reorganizing a calculation changes its cost (Cooley and Tukey 1965). Trefethen’s approximation text gives a gentle route from polynomial approximation to spectral accuracy (Trefethen 2013).

Cooley, James W., and John W. Tukey. 1965. “An Algorithm for the Machine Calculation of Complex Fourier Series.” Mathematics of Computation 19 (90): 297–301. https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0178586-1.
Trefethen, Lloyd N. 2013. Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics.
